title: Wells, Oaths and a Curse
sum: After Abraham's death the blessing passes to Isaac. A famine comes, and Esau, coming in hungry, sells his birthright to Jacob for bread and stew, sealing it with an oath; Jubilees states the result plainly: "Jacob became the elder" (24:7). Isaac sets out for Egypt but God stops him at Gerar and repeats the promise to Abraham. He grows rich among the Philistines, reopens Abraham's wells and names new ones, and comes up to the Well of the Oath, where God appears to him on New Year's Day.

The chapter then turns sharply. Isaac's servants find no water after his oath of peace with the Philistines, and Isaac realizes he swore under pressure. He curses the Philistines with a curse built on Amos 9: no remnant, no escape in sky, earth or Sheol. The angel adds that the curse is engraved on the heavenly tablets.
readings: Read as a retelling of Genesis

Jubilees follows Genesis 25:29–26:33 closely but reorders it (the famine comes before the stew), leaves out Isaac's lie about Rebekah, makes the birthright a fair sale, and reads Genesis 26:32 as "they did not find water." Each change makes Isaac and Jacob look better and the Philistines worse.
Read as a word for the author's own day

The curse on the Philistines has no root in Genesis. Charles argued that it makes sense only in the time of the Maccabean wars, when Judas and Jonathan fought and burned the Philistine cities (1 Maccabees 5:68; 1 Maccabees 10:84). On this reading Isaac's words bless a war the first readers knew.

views.E: For the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church this is part of Kufale, read as Scripture alongside Genesis. The chapter fills out Genesis 26 and teaches that God's judgments are written in heaven before they happen.
views.H: The author smooths Genesis here, leaving out Isaac's lie about Rebekah, and adds a curse Genesis does not have. Charles thought the curse "hardly intelligible save in a contemporary of the wars waged by the Maccabeans against the Philistine cities," and used it as a clue to the book's date.
views.N: Esau's sale of the birthright is the scene Hebrews 12:16 uses as a warning. The promise that the nations "will be blessed" in Abraham's offspring is quoted the same way in Acts 3:25 and Galatians 3:8.
views.J: Jubilees reads Genesis 26:32 as "they did not find water," as the Septuagint, the Jewish Greek translation, does; Charles notes that the Hebrew, Samaritan and Syriac read lo, "to him," where these have lo', "not."
views.W: Most Christian readers value the chapter as an early Jewish reading of Genesis 26, while noting that its curse on the Philistines goes far beyond Genesis and that Genesis 26:28–31 ends Isaac's dealings with Abimelech in peace.

Amos 9:2–4 says that Israel's sinners cannot hide from God in Sheol, in the heavens, on Carmel, in the sea or in captivity. Charles showed that Isaac's curse borrows this pattern (24:31–32). The same images in Psalm 139:7–10 comfort the believer: God is there too. Jubilees gives the threat to Israel's enemy. Obadiah 4 uses the same picture against Edom, the nation descended from Esau.

B.C."

title: A Mother's Charge and Blessing
sum: Before any blessing is stolen, Rebekah calls Jacob and warns him not to marry a Canaanite as Esau did. Jacob, now sixty-three, answers with a vow: he has never been with a woman, Abraham warned him against lust and sexual immorality, and for twenty-two years he has refused Esau's urging to marry one of his wives' sisters. He will marry from his mother's family in Haran.

Rebekah lifts her hands and blesses God, and a spirit of righteousness comes into her mouth. With her hands on Jacob's head she blesses him in a poem: twelve sons, offspring past counting, the good land, God dwelling with them and his sanctuary built among them forever. Genesis gives such blessings only to fathers; Jubilees gives one to a mother.
readings: Read as a story of character

The chapter makes Jacob the model young man: chaste, obedient to his mother, faithful to Abraham's teaching, the opposite of Esau. That is why, in Jubilees, he deserves the blessing that follows in chapter 26.
Read as teaching for Israel
Rebekah's charge and Jacob's vow teach the first readers to marry within Israel. The prayer that Jacob's offspring be "holy" anticipates the strong law of chapter 30.

views.E: The Ethiopian church reads Kufale as Scripture; here it gives honor to Rebekah as one who blesses by the spirit, a picture of a mother's prayer for her son.
views.H: Charles notes that the author moved Genesis 28:1–4 before Genesis 27 and gave the charge to Rebekah. The chapter belongs with the book's teaching against marriage with Gentiles, which reaches its height in 30:7–17.
views.N: Rebekah's blessing shares wording with Luke 1:55 ("to Abraham and his offspring for all time"), as Charles noticed. The "spirit of righteousness" may stand for the "spirit of truth" (John 14:17).
views.J: Charles cites Genesis Rabbah 68, which also makes Jacob sixty-three when he received the blessing, and then eighty-four when he married. He notes that the age of sixty-three does not fit Jubilees everywhere: it puts Jacob's birth in 2046 from creation, while 45:13 puts it in 2041.
views.W: Most Christian readers find in Rebekah's prayer a moving picture of a mother's faith, while noting that Genesis does not report it.

deep.b: Jubilees counts Jacob's age in "weeks" of years. Nine weeks is 63. Esau married at 40 (Genesis 26:34), so his wives have been with him 22 years (25:8). Charles points out that the two numbers agree.

echoes: Genesis 26:34–35; Genesis 27:46; Genesis 28:1–4; Genesis 12:2–3; Genesis 27:29; Luke 1:55; Ezra 9:2; Exodus 34:16; Deuteronomy 7:3

settings.what: Rebekah's charge not to marry a Canaanite
settings.when: in the second year of the week, while Esau's Canaanite wives grieve her
settings.why: to keep Jacob from Esau's path and to see his children become a righteous generation and a holy offspring

settings.what: Jacob's vow to marry within the family
settings.when: in reply to her charge, at sixty-three
settings.why: to assure his mother that he has kept himself pure and will marry one of Laban's daughters, as Abraham commanded

settings.by: Rebekah, by a spirit of righteousness
settings.when: right after Jacob's vow
settings.why: to thank God for a pure son and to call down on Jacob the promises of Abraham: many sons, the land, God's presence and his sanctuary
settings.readers: The prayer that God's sanctuary be built among Jacob's offspring "for all the ages" spoke to readers for whom the temple in Jerusalem was the center of life.

title: The Stolen Blessing
sum: Isaac, old and nearly blind, sends Esau to hunt so that he may bless him. Rebekah overhears and sends Jacob in with two young goats, Esau's clothes and goatskins on his hands and neck. Isaac feels him, hears Jacob's voice, and blesses him with dew, grain, rule over his brothers and the blessings of Abraham. Esau returns, cries out bitterly, and receives only a word about living by the sword.

The story follows Genesis 27 closely, but every change helps Jacob. He never says "I am Esau," only "I am your son." Heaven itself takes away Isaac's discernment "so that he would bless him" (26:18). And Esau's future changes: when he throws off Jacob's yoke he will sin unto death and his offspring will be uprooted (26:34).
readings: Read as a defense of Jacob

Jubilees removes Jacob's plain lies (Genesis 27:19, 24), adds his care for his father (26:7), and makes God the one who blinds Isaac. Charles shows that later rabbis also explained away Jacob's words (Genesis Rabbah 65).
Read as a story about God's choice

Genesis already says the elder will serve the younger (Genesis 25:23). Jubilees presses the point: the blessing went where heaven meant it to go. Paul makes a similar point about God's choice in Romans 9:10–13.

views.E: For the Ethiopian church the chapter, as Scripture in Kufale, teaches that God's purpose stood behind Jacob's blessing.
views.H: The author removes the moral problem of Genesis 27 and turns Esau, the ancestor of Edom, into a figure doomed to a "sin unto death." Charles calls this change to Genesis 27:40 "contrary to all tradition." The book later tells of Esau's war against Jacob (chapters 37–38).
views.N: Hebrews 11:20 calls Isaac's blessing an act of faith, and Hebrews 12:17 says Esau "found no place for repentance." Romans 9:10–13 uses Jacob and Esau for God's choice.
views.J: Charles notes that the Targum Onkelos reads Genesis 27:40 the opposite way: Esau will throw off the yoke when Jacob's sons break the law. Jubilees' version has no parallel in that tradition.
views.W: Most Christian readers take Genesis 27 as an honest account of a flawed family through whom God still worked. Jubilees' softer Jacob is an early example of the wish to make the fathers blameless.

settings.why: to send Esau to hunt and make him a meal, so that Isaac may bless him before he dies

settings.readers: The blessing, read with 26:18, assured the first readers that Israel, not Edom, holds Abraham's blessing by heaven's will.

settings.when: after Esau begs for a blessing
settings.why: to tell Esau his lot: away from the dew, living by the sword, serving his brother, and doomed if he throws off the yoke

title: Flight and the Stairway to Heaven
sum: A dream tells Rebekah that Esau plans to kill Jacob. Jacob is not afraid and would fight, but he will not leave his blind father without his consent, so Rebekah persuades Isaac. Isaac blesses Jacob, sends him to Mesopotamia to marry one of Laban's daughters, and then comforts Rebekah, his "sister," who weeps for her son: Jacob is upright and blameless, and he will return in peace.

On the way, on New Year's Day, Jacob sleeps at Luz. He dreams of a stairway reaching to heaven with the angels of the Lord going up and down, and the Lord standing on it, who repeats the promises of land, offspring and protection. Jacob names the place Bethel, "house of the Lord," and vows a tenth of all he will receive.
readings: Read as a family story
Jubilees fills Genesis 27:42–28:22 with feeling: a son's respect for his father, a mother's tears, a husband's tenderness. Isaac and Rebekah act together, not at cross purposes as in Genesis 27.
Read as the start of Bethel's story
The vow of a tenth at Bethel (27:27) prepares for Jacob's return there (31:1–3) and for Levi's ordination and the tithes in chapter 32.

views.E: As Scripture in Kufale for the Ethiopian church, the chapter adds to Genesis 28 Isaac's comforting words and the date of Jacob's dream, New Year's Day.
views.H: Charles, following Singer, saw 27:6 as a defense of Jacob against the charge that he abandoned his parents, a charge known from later rabbinic texts.
views.N: Jesus takes up Jacob's dream: "you will see heaven standing open, and God's angels going up and coming down on the Son of Man" (John 1:51).
views.J: Charles notes that Targum Pseudo-Jonathan and Genesis Rabbah also gave Rebekah prophetic knowledge, as Jubilees' dream does.
views.W: Most Christian readers see Bethel as a picture of God's faithfulness to the undeserving, and of Christ as the true way between earth and heaven (John 1:51).

deep.b: In Genesis 27 Isaac and Rebekah work against each other. In Jubilees they act together. Rebekah blesses Jacob (25:11–23), persuades Isaac to send him (27:7–8), and weeps when he goes; Isaac calls her "my sister," a tender address (Charles compares Tobit 5:21 and Song of Songs 4:9), and assures her that Jacob is "upright," "blameless" and "faithful" (27:17). The book presents the parents of Israel as united in wanting their son to marry within the family.

echoes: Genesis 27:42–28:22; Genesis 25:27; John 1:51; Genesis 35:6–7; Genesis 14:20; Hebrews 7:4

settings.when: after a dream reveals Esau's plan
settings.why: to send Jacob to Laban until Esau's anger cools

settings.when: as Jacob leaves for Mesopotamia
settings.why: to forbid a Canaanite wife, send him to Bethuel's house and give him Abraham's blessing and the land

settings.when: as she weeps after Jacob leaves
settings.why: to assure her that God Most High will guard their upright son and bring him back in peace

settings.by: the Lord, standing on the stairway
settings.when: on the first day of the first month
settings.why: to give Jacob the promises of Abraham and Isaac and to promise to be with him and bring him back

settings.when: the morning after the dream
settings.why: to bind himself to worship the Lord at Bethel and give a tenth of all he receives
settings.readers: The vow prepared the first readers for the account of tithes and of Levi's priesthood in chapter 32, which the book uses to ground the priests' share.

title: Two Wives and Eleven Children
sum: Jacob serves Laban a week of years for Rachel, but Laban gives him Leah. The angel breaks into the story to declare a law from the heavenly tablets: a younger daughter may not be given in marriage before an older one. A week later Jacob receives Rachel too, and serves seven more years.

Then come the births, each with an exact date: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah to Leah; Dan and Naphtali to Bilhah; Gad and Asher to Zilpah; Issachar, and twins Zebulun and Dinah, to Leah; at last Joseph to Rachel. Jacob asks to go home, takes the marked lambs and kids as his wages, and grows rich without any trick with peeled branches. Laban and his sons grow jealous.
readings: Read as chronology
Jubilees dates every birth to the day, by its own calendar of jubilees and weeks. Charles judged several dates corrupt, since Dan is dated before Judah. The table below sets them out.
Read as law

The marriage of Leah and Rachel becomes the occasion for a new law about the order of daughters' marriages, though Jubilees says nothing of Leviticus 18:18, which forbids marrying two sisters together.

views.E: The Ethiopian church receives Kufale as Scripture; the chapter supplies dates and details for Genesis 29–30 that Genesis does not give.
views.H: The law about older daughters, Charles reports, has "no hint" in other Jewish tradition. The chapter shows the author's habit of finding laws behind stories, and of tidying the patriarchs' lives.
views.N: The twelve sons are the roots of the twelve tribes, which the New Testament takes up in the twelve apostles and the twelve gates of the new Jerusalem (Matthew 19:28; Revelation 21:12).
views.J: Charles notes that Midrash Tadshe, a later Hebrew work, gives the same days and months for several births, and that later Jewish tradition made Bilhah and Zilpah sisters, as Jubilees does.
views.W: Most Christian readers take the chapter as a witness to how Jews before Christ read Genesis 29–30, and do not treat its new marriage law as binding.

deep.b:
All dates fall in the forty-fourth jubilee. The year from creation is worked out from the book's own formula (43 × 49 + weeks + years); Charles prints the same figures in his margin.

settings.what: The law about older and younger daughters
settings.by: the angel of the presence, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai
settings.to: Moses, to be commanded to the Israelites
settings.when: breaking into the story of Laban's trick
settings.why: to declare from the heavenly tablets that a father must give his older daughter in marriage before the younger, and that whoever does otherwise has guilt recorded in heaven
settings.readers: The law bound fathers in Israel who arranged their daughters' marriages. Charles notes it has no parallel in other Jewish tradition, so it is one of the book's own rulings.

title: Home to Canaan
sum: While Laban is away shearing, Jacob wins over Leah and Rachel and sets out with his family and flocks for Gilead. Laban overtakes him on Mount Gilead, but the Lord has warned Laban in a dream. The two make a feast and an oath on the fifteenth of the third month, and set up the Heap of Witness. The angel adds that Gilead was once the land of the Rephaim, giants destroyed by the Lord, whose place the wicked Amorites took.

Jacob crosses the Jabbok and makes peace with Esau in a single sentence: no wrestling, no new name, no gifts. He settles beyond the Jordan and sends food and clothing to Isaac four times a year, and gifts to Rebekah, at Abraham's tower in Hebron. Esau, by contrast, has married Mahalath, taken his father's flocks and left Isaac alone.
readings: Read as a retelling
Jubilees compresses Genesis 31–33 into twenty verses. What it keeps shows its interests: the covenant with Laban, God's protection, the land's old giants, and Jacob as a dutiful son.
Read as a map of Maccabean victories

Charles thought the list of Rephaim cities (29:10) named places where Judas Maccabee had fought, such as Karnaim and Beon (1 Maccabees 5:4–5, 43–44). Of Jacob's grazing lands (29:14) he linked Akrabbim with Akrabattene, where Judas fought the Edomites (1 Maccabees 5:3), and said Beth-shan was linked with Judas only "in a peaceful way."

views.E: For the Ethiopian church this chapter of Kufale adds to Genesis 31–33 the giants of Gilead and Jacob's care for his parents.
views.H: The omission of the wrestling at the Jabbok is striking. The comment that the Amorites "no longer have long life" may reflect the author's own day, as Charles thought.
views.N: The care Jacob shows his parents illustrates the commandment to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12), which Paul calls "the first commandment that comes with a promise" (Ephesians 6:2).
views.J: Charles notes that later rabbinic texts blamed Jacob for staying away from his parents; Jubilees makes him send them gifts four times a year.
views.W: Most Christian readers notice what is missing: Jacob's wrestling with God (Genesis 32:22–32), one of the most-read scenes in Genesis, where he receives the name Israel.

deep.h: What Jubilees leaves out of Genesis 31–33
deep.b: Laban's search for his household gods (Genesis 31:30–35); Jacob's complaint of twenty years' hard service (Genesis 31:36–42); the angels of God at Mahanaim (Genesis 32:1–2); Jacob's fear, prayer and gifts for Esau (Genesis 32:3–21); the wrestling at the Jabbok and the name Israel (Genesis 32:22–32); the meeting with Esau and his four hundred men (Genesis 33:1–16). Jubilees gives Jacob's new name at Bethel in chapter 32, following Genesis 35:10.
A cubit is the length of a forearm, about 18 inches. The Rephaim of 29:9, at seven to ten cubits, would be about ten and a half to fifteen feet tall.

echoes: Genesis 31:3–33:20; Genesis 14:5; Deuteronomy 2:11; Deuteronomy 3:11; Genesis 15:16; Genesis 28:9; Exodus 20:12

settings.what: The angel's note on the Rephaim
settings.by: the angel of the presence, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai
settings.when: after the covenant at the Heap of Witness
settings.why: to explain Gilead's old name and to say that the Lord destroyed the giant Rephaim and that the Amorites who followed them have filled up their sins
settings.readers: Charles read "today" (29:11) as the author's own time, when Judas Maccabee fought in Gilead and Bashan; the note would then assure readers that those wars carried out God's judgment.

title: Dinah and the Zeal of Levi
sum: At Salem near Shechem, Dinah, a twelve-year-old girl, is carried off into Shechem's house and defiled. Shechem asks to marry her; Jacob and his sons answer with deceit, and Simeon and Levi kill every man of the city. Jubilees leaves out the circumcision of the Shechemites and says the judgment was decreed in heaven.

Then the angel lays down the law: a man who gives his daughter or sister to a Gentile is to be stoned, the woman burned; this is giving one's offspring to Molech; there is no atonement for it, and a whole people that looks away will be judged. Because Levi was zealous, his offspring were chosen for the priesthood, and his righteousness is written on the heavenly tablets. Jacob only "spoke with them," and the terror of the Lord kept the cities from pursuing.
readings: Read as law

This is the book's strongest teaching against marriage with outsiders. Charles shows how it is built from Leviticus 18:21 and 20:2–5 (Molech) and from the burning of Tamar (Genesis 38:24) and a priest's daughter (Leviticus 21:9).
Read against Genesis

Genesis tells the story with moral unease: Jacob rebukes his sons (Genesis 34:30) and later curses their anger (Genesis 49:5–7). Jubilees removes the unease. Charles shows that other Jewish writings of the time, such as Judith 9:2 and the Testament of Levi, also praised the deed, while later rabbis judged it by Genesis 49.

views.E: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church reads Kufale as Scripture. This chapter grounds the Levitical priesthood in Levi's zeal; how the church applies its marriage law is not stated in the sources used here.
views.H: Charles thought the chapter's reading of Leviticus 18:21 as marriage to a Gentile "may not be older than the Maccabean age." He adds that the author enlarges guilt from one man to the whole people (30:15) to justify the killing of every Shechemite.
views.N: Paul tells believers, "Do not hitch yourselves to unbelievers in a yoke that does not match" (2 Corinthians 6:14), but also tells a believer married to an unbeliever to stay if the spouse is willing (1 Corinthians 7:12–14), a very different spirit from Jubilees 30.
views.J: Charles shows that the reading of Leviticus 18:21 as marriage to a Gentile appears in Targum Pseudo-Jonathan, while the Mishnah (Megillah 4:9) orders that whoever translates it so be silenced.
views.W: Most Christian readers see in Genesis 34 a story of sin on every side, and read Jubilees' praise of the massacre and its death penalties as going far beyond the Bible.

deep.b: The Bible holds two pictures of Levi. Genesis 49:5–7 curses the anger of Simeon and Levi and scatters them in Israel. But the Levites are set apart for God after they kill the worshipers of the golden calf (Exodus 32:26–29), Moses blesses Levi for keeping God's covenant (Deuteronomy 33:8–11), and Malachi praises God's "covenant with Levi" (Malachi 2:4–7). Phinehas, Levi's descendant, receives "a covenant of priesthood for all time" for his zeal against an Israelite who took a Midianite woman (Numbers 25:13). Jubilees reads Shechem in the light of Phinehas: Levi's zeal against a marriage with outsiders "was counted to them as righteousness" (30:17; Psalm 106:31), and his line is chosen for the priesthood. Charles notes that Jubilees itself gives another reason in 32:3.

deep.title: Claude's theory: why Dinah is "twelve"
deep.b: This is Claude's theory. By Jubilees' own dates Dinah would be about nine at 30:1 (born 2134, 28:23; the event in 2143). The text says twelve. The number may come from a tradition the author shared with the Testament of Levi, where Levi is eighteen (Charles notes the agreement), rather than from the book's own arithmetic. If so, the dates of chapter 28 and the age here come from different sources. I have not found this discussed in the sources opened for this part.

echoes: Genesis 33:18–35:5; Genesis 49:5–7; Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 20:2–5; Leviticus 21:9; Deuteronomy 7:3; Numbers 25:6–13; Psalm 106:30–31; Judith 9:2; Ezra 9–10; 2 Corinthians 6:14

settings.what: The law against giving daughters to the nations
settings.by: the angel of the presence, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai
settings.to: Moses, to command and warn the Israelites
settings.when: after the slaughter at Shechem
settings.why: to forbid every marriage between Israelites and Gentiles: death by stoning for the father, burning for the woman, no atonement, and judgment on a whole people that looks away
settings.readers: The law bound every Israelite father and the community that judged him. Charles thought its reading of Leviticus 18:21 as marriage to a Gentile "may not be older than the Maccabean age," when "the circumstances of that time were such as to justify the extremest measures in order to save Judaism from annihilation." He notes that the Mishnah (Megillah 4:9) later ordered anyone who translated the verse that way to be silenced.

settings.by: the angel of the presence, speaking to Moses on Mount Sinai
settings.when: continuing the law
settings.why: to explain that Levi's line was chosen for the priesthood because of his zeal, and to call Israel to keep the covenant and be recorded as friends
settings.readers: Genesis 49:5–7 condemns Simeon and Levi's deed at Shechem. Yet Charles, citing the Testament of Levi 5–6 and Judith 9:2, notes that the deed "was highly extolled in the two centuries preceding the Christian era." The passage spoke to Jews who already honored that zeal.

title: Isaac Blesses Levi and Judah
sum: Jacob purifies his household, destroys the foreign gods and Rachel's stolen idols, and goes up to Bethel on the first day of the seventh month to pay his vow. He visits his parents at Abraham's tower with two of his sons, Levi and Judah. Rebekah's spirit revives; the darkness leaves Isaac's eyes, and a spirit of prophecy comes upon him.

Isaac blesses Levi first: his sons will serve in God's sanctuary like the angels of the presence, rule, judge, teach Jacob God's ways and bless Israel. Then he blesses Judah: power over his enemies, rule for him and "one of your sons," and in him the help and salvation of Israel. Too old to go to Bethel, Isaac sends Rebekah with Jacob, and Jacob rejoices that these blessings are written on the heavenly tablets.
readings: Read as a blessing of two offices
Priesthood and kingship, Levi and Judah, stand side by side, with the priest first. Charles saw the Hasmonean priest-rulers in Levi's line, and a messiah from Judah in "one of your sons."
Read in the Christian canon
Christians read the two blessings together in Jesus, who is from Judah (Hebrews 7:14) and is also priest, "after the pattern of Melchizedek" rather than of Levi (Hebrews 7:17).

views.E: As Scripture in Kufale, this chapter honors both the priesthood and the royal line of Judah. The Ethiopian church's own book-level discussion is in book.json.
views.H: Charles argued that Levi's double role of priest and ruler "requires us to recognise the early Maccabean princes," and that the Testament of Levi 8 shares the tradition.
views.N: Hebrews 7 contrasts the Levitical priesthood with Christ's, from Judah. Revelation calls Jesus "the Lion from the tribe of Judah" (Revelation 5:5).
views.J: Charles shows that the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs look for a leader from Levi (Testament of Levi 18) or from Judah (Testament of Judah 24). The pairing of Levi and Judah was common in Jewish hopes of this time.
views.W: Most Christian readers find the chapter a valuable witness to Jewish hopes for a priest and a king, which the New Testament sees joined in Christ.

deep.title: Claude's theory: right hand and left hand
deep.b: This is Claude's theory. The order of honor is shown twice: Isaac takes Levi by the right hand and Judah by the left before blessing them (31:12), and that night he has them sleep at his right and left (31:23). Genesis 48:13–14 uses the same right and left hands for Ephraim's precedence over Manasseh. Jubilees seems to stage Levi's precedence over Judah the same way, so that the priest outranks the king. Charles notes only that Levi is blessed first.

echoes: Genesis 35:1–8; Genesis 49:5–12; Deuteronomy 33:7–11; Malachi 2:4–7; Numbers 18:1–20; Hebrews 7:11–17; Revelation 5:5; Genesis 45:27

settings.to: all the people of his household
settings.when: on the first day of the month, before going to Bethel
settings.why: to prepare his household to worship at Bethel by washing, changing clothes and putting away foreign gods

settings.what: Rebekah's blessing of Levi and Judah
settings.when: on meeting her grandsons at the tower
settings.why: to bless them as those through whom Abraham's offspring will be honored

settings.by: Isaac, by a spirit of prophecy
settings.when: at Abraham's tower, with Jacob present
settings.why: to give Levi's line the priesthood, the right to rule and judge, the task of teaching and blessing Israel, and a share of the Lord's table
settings.readers: Charles read the blessing as written for the time of the Hasmonean priest-princes, who were high priests and rulers together; it would give their rule a blessing from Isaac himself.

settings.when: right after Levi's blessing
settings.why: to give Judah's line power, rule and the salvation of Israel, with "one of your sons" as ruler
settings.readers: Charles thought readers would hear a messiah from Judah in "one of your sons," though he saw no active role for that figure in the book's gradual kingdom.

settings.what: Isaac's charge to keep the vow
settings.when: the morning after the blessings
settings.why: to send Jacob, with Rebekah, to pay his vow at Bethel without delay

settings.to: the God of his fathers, at Bethel
settings.when: after he remembers Isaac's blessing of Levi and Judah
settings.why: to say that he and his sons have an eternal hope before the God of all; the angel adds that it is recorded on the heavenly tablets
